title: Smallest Range Around Each Point
statement:
You get a list of ranges, ranges[i] = [left, right], each covering the integers from left to right inclusive. The size of a range is the number of integers it covers, right − left + 1.

You also get a list of points. For each point, find the smallest size of any range that contains it, or -1 if no range does. Return the answers in the same order as points.

examples.why: At 5, [4, 5] (size 2) wins. At 7, the small ranges have already ended and only [1, 9] (size 9) is left. Nothing covers 10.
A single-number range has size 1. Repeated points get their own answer each, in their original slots.
The small range [50, 51] starts late and ends early. Points before it and after it both fall back to [1, 100].

hints: Checking every range for every point is O(n · q), too slow for 10⁵ of each. The answers do not depend on the order you compute them in. Would a different order help?

Handle the points from smallest to largest. As the point moves right, ranges start covering it (their left is now ≤ the point) and later stop (their right is now < the point). Each range enters and leaves once.

Sort ranges by left and the point indices by value. For each point: push every range whose left ≤ point into a min-heap keyed by size; pop from the top while the top's right < point; the top's size is the answer. Write it into the point's original slot.

explain.intuition:
Nothing forces you to answer the points in the order they are given. Answering them offline, sorted from smallest to largest, turns the problem into a sweep. As the point moves right, ranges become "open" once their left is reached, and they become useless forever once their right is passed, because every later point is even further right.

Keep the open ranges in a min-heap by size. For each point, first push every range that has started. Then look at the top: if it already ended before this point, it is useless now and later, so pop it and look again. When the top covers the point, its size is the answer. Ranges deeper in the heap that have also ended are harmless: they are removed when they reach the top. This is lazy deletion, the same trick as skipping stale entries in Dijkstra. Each range is pushed and popped at most once, so the sweep is O((n + q) log n) after sorting. Remember each point's original index, so the answers go back into the right slots.
steps: Sort ranges by left. Sort the indices of points by value.
For each point p in that order: while the next range has left ≤ p, push (size, right) into a min-heap.
While the heap's top has right < p, pop it: it has ended and cannot help any later point.
Write the top's size into answer[original index], or -1 if the heap is empty.
pitfalls: Returning the answers in sorted order instead of the original order of points.
Popping a range just because it is not needed for the current point. Only ranges whose right is below the point are dead; the rest may be the answer for a later point.
Forgetting the + 1 in the size: [3, 3] has size 1, not 0.

complexity.time: O(n log n + q log q)

solutions.title: Check every range for every point
solutions.idea: For each point, scan all ranges and keep the smallest that covers it.

solutions.title: Sorted points with a min-heap of open ranges
solutions.idea: Sweep the points left to right. Push ranges as they start, keyed by size; drop ended ranges lazily from the top; the top is the answer.
solutions.time: O(n log n + q log q)

followups: The points arrive one at a time and must be answered immediately (online). What changes, and what structure could you use?
Another approach sorts the ranges by size and gives each one to all still-unanswered points it covers. How do you skip already-answered points quickly? (Think union-find over the sorted points.)
